In recent weeks and months, Russia has intensified its airstrikes on Ukraine , regularly firing dozens of ballistic missiles and drones, often at civilian targets. To defend itself, Ukraine relies on advanced, foreign-made weapons systems — most importantly, US Patriot missiles . The US war with Iran has depleted its own stockpiles, and Washington has resisted providing Kyiv with large numbers of missiles , leaving Ukraine more exposed to Russian bombs. Even before the war with Iran, US support for Ukraine had wavered after Donald Trump returned to the White House in 2025. Trump, who had an angry public spat with Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy at the White House , has sought to mend ties with Russia's Vladimir Putin , and ordered a pause of US military aid to Kyiv . Over the weekend, Zelenskyy revealed that deliveries of Patriot interceptors had dropped by 50% since 2023. "Over the entire year of 2023, Ukraine received 675 missiles, and over all of 2025 — 364, even though Russian missile strikes have increased," he said. "For 2026, as currently projected, it is 264." Is the US running out of weapons? Photograph: Anadolu/Getty Images View image in fullscreen Loui Ridi looks on as Palestinian residents are confined in their homes in the village of Qusra, south of Nablus in the West Bank, on 20 August 2026. Photograph: Anadolu/Getty Images Ohio In a town in the heart of the US, Israeli settler violence in West Bank hits close to home War on Gaza and violence in West Bank is playing out in the streets of Toledo, Ohio, where the Arab American community has flourished Stephen Starr in Toledo, Ohio Mon 31 Aug 2026 07.00 EDT Last modified on Mon 31 Aug 2026 07.01 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google From his office outside Toledo, Ohio, Thamin Tim Ridi opens his phone to livestream the scene outside the besieged house of his brother, Loui, thousands of miles away in the occupied West Bank . This month, with his property at risk of being destroyed by Israeli settlers, Loui traveled from Ohio to his ancestral home in Qusra , south of Nablus, where his mother and other family members have been living in constant fear of attack. In Qusra, settlers have besieged a number of Palestinian properties and homes, preventing members of the Ridi family from leaving, as their food and water supplies dwindled. The US ambassador to Israel, Mike Huckabee, took to X on 13 August to describe the settlers’ actions as those of “terrorists”. While the Trump administration has offered broad support to Israel and its illegal settlement building over the years, recent comments from JD Vance, the vice-president, and Donald Trump himself indicate a change of tone. On scraps of land and under constant threat, Gaza farmers struggle to survive Read more Regardless, for Loui’s extended family in Ohio , it’s created a world of concern. “This building has been taken by settlers; that one up there by the soldiers,” Ridi said, pointing at the outline of buildings further up the hill from his brother’s home that are barely visible on his phone. “I’m extremely worried about them,” he said, his eyes clued to the security camera footage that’s coming through his phone. One of the first things Loui did upon arriving at his home in Qusra, said Ridi, was plant an American flag on his property. For decades, the war in the Middle East had been a distant headline, something that appeared briefly on the evening news, for residents of Toledo in north-west Ohio. But decades of migration to small cities in the American heartland, combined with the war on Gaza and recent rise in settler violence against Palestinians in the occupied West Bank, are bringing the conflict into the streets and homes of places such as Toledo. Last October, five people were arrested in downtown Toledo for protesting outside the office of Jon Husted, an Ohio Republican senator, who at the time had voted to send aid to Israel. “There’s been demonstrations, petitions and the city council passed a resolution calling for a ceasefire not long after October 7 [2023]. There’s a palpable difference of opinion regarding what Israel is doing and that the US is funding it,” said Mike Ferner, a US navy veteran and one of those arrested in Toledo. Ferner said he began speaking out against America’s support for Israel after the war on Gaza began. “It just comes to a point where you have to ask: is this what I want my country paying for?” Israel’s military assault has largely destroyed the Gaza Strip and killed more than 76,000 people while being condemned by a United Nations body as a genocide . It has prompted Ferner to travel to New York City and organize a 40-day fast in front of the United Nations building last year. “We made our point as best we could that this is something dreadful and the US has got no business participating in it,” he says. Ferner’s position is illustrative of a widening gap between American public opinion and the US government’s support for Israel. While Americans broadly supported Israel in the past, a Pew Research Center poll released in April found that six in 10 participants had an unfavorable view of the country – an increase of 7% in just a year. The reason is partly explained by mounting anger with the actions of pro-Israel groups such as American Israel Public Affairs Committee (Aipac), which have spent billions of dollars over a period of decades helping to elect American politicians who are supportive of Israel. This year, many of its high-profile candidates have been defeated in primary elections, despite an outlay of tens of millions of dollars. Arab American communities have grown particularly in the midwest, where job opportunities and a comparatively affordable cost of living have attracted many immigrants to start out. Aside from English and Spanish, Arabic is the most popular primary language spoken in Ohio. Drawn to the region’s growing manufacturing industry in the early 20th century, Toledo once had its own “ Little Syria ” district, located in the Old North End neighborhood. “Since the late 1800s, people would come here, work at Cooper Tire and then retire back in Lebanon; my great-grandparents did that, everyone did it,” says Nabil Shaheen, who as a child emigrated from Lebanon with his mother, brother and sister in 1979, and also worked in manufacturing. “There are at least 300 families from Sultan Yacub [Shaheen’s village in Lebanon] here. We even have a Sultan Yacub club, which for every occasion we meet there.” Today, he and his family run a sign manufacturing company west of downtown Toledo. “This used to be a church, then it was empty, and we came in. There’s a variety of [Arab American] businesses that are contributing to the city of Toledo,” he says from his office, which has wall-to-wall paraphernalia of the Cincinnati Bengals NFL team. Today, many Arab Americans in the area have moved to suburban Sylvania west of Toledo, where eastern Orthodox churches, a mosque and an Islamic school have opened in recent decades. In these communities, away from the conflict, dialogue between Arab and Jewish Americans has flourished. “As a Jewish community, we believe deeply in the importance of a shared society: one grounded in respect for diversity, the dignity and rights of every individual,” says Roy Büchler of the Jewish Federation of Greater Toledo. “Loui [Ridi] and his brother have built successful businesses, created jobs, paid taxes, supported numerous philanthropic causes, and worked to build bridges among people of different backgrounds throughout our community.” However, the federation declined to comment on the settler violence. Founded in 1999, the Ridi family’s chain of supermarkets, car washes and gas stations stretch out across north-west Ohio, Michigan and Indiana after several of the brothers came to the US to attend university during the 1990s. The company, which employs hundreds of people, forms the cornerstone of Toledo’s bustling Palestinian American community and donates hundreds of thousands of dollars every year to charities and nonprofits. Ridi said he typically visits Qusra three times a year, taking his children, but the war on Gaza and violence in the occupied West Bank have made that harder in recent years. Still, he is not without hope for change. “I was so surprised by [US ambassador] Huckabee’s comments, calling the settlers Israeli terrorists ,” he said. “Maybe something is changing.” Explore more on these topics Ohio West Bank Palestine features Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed US news US politics Midterms 2026 World Climate crisis Middle East Ukraine US immigration Soccer Business Environment Tech Science Newsletters The Filter Wellness

Photograph: AP South Africa ‘We are prey’: discovery of seven women’s bodies fuels anger over femicide in South Africa String of female murder victims found near Johannesburg’s international airport, including five in the past week Rachel Savage in Johannesburg Wed 16 Sep 2026 03.00 EDT Last modified on Wed 16 Sep 2026 03.01 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The discovery of the bodies of seven women around Johannesburg’s international airport, including five in the past week, has prompted an outpouring of fear, grief and anger over a lack of progress in tackling femicide. When Elizabeth “Tsontso” Moselakgomo did not return after going for a run on 9 September, her eight-year-old daughter alerted relatives, who contacted police. The 38-year-old’s body was found on Saturday and identified by relatives on Monday. The news of her disappearance had gone viral. Police said in a statement on Saturday that four women’s bodies had been found since 15 July in Kempton Park, across the highway from OR Tambo international airport. All were half-naked and with visible bruising. On Monday and Tuesday, two more bodies were found in Olifantsfontein, about 15 miles north of Kempton Park. On Tuesday, police said another woman’s body had been found 25 miles to the south-east, naked and decomposed. “In this country we are prey,” Sakane Mokoena posted on Instagram after confirmation of the death of her friend and fellow runner Moselakgomo. Elizabeth Moselakgomo was abducted and killed while out for a run on 9 September. South Africa has one of the highest rates of femicide in the world. In the year to 31 March 2024, more than 27,600 people were murdered, 5,578 of them women, according to the latest police data . For years, women have called on the South African government to take gender-based violence seriously . After hundreds of women protested on the eve of the G20 summit in Johannesburg in November 2025, President Cyril Ramaphosa declared it a national crisis. However, the lack of a concrete plan or action has frustrated campaigners – and women keep being killed. The latest deaths are being investigated by specialist officers, who said on Saturday: “Women in and around Kempton Park are urged not to walk or run alone, particularly in isolated areas. They should avoid secluded spaces, remain vigilant and, where possible, travel or exercise in groups.” South African women responded with anger at the idea that they had to be responsible for their own safety, with many runners noting they already took precautions, such as sharing routes. “We are tired of being told to be vigilant when women are already doing everything possible to stay alive,” said the advocacy group Women For Change . “It should not take a missing woman, a desperate family, runners and communities searching, and a case going viral, before an area is searched with this intensity,” the group said. Detectives said on Saturday that they were examining a serial killer angle. However, on Monday, a police spokesperson, Athlenda Mathe, told reporters : “For now, nothing tells us that we’ve got a serial killer.” Mathe added that a suspect in the killing in July of the first woman, her boyfriend, was in custody. Ramaphosa said on Tuesday that he had directed police authorities to prioritise the ongoing murder investigations. Although the gender of the suspect or suspects in the other killings has not been confirmed, campaigners called on men to take responsibility for violence against women and children. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to The Long Wave Nesrine Malik, Micha Frazer-Carroll and the team guide you through the biggest Black stories from around the world after newsletter promotion View image in fullscreen A protest against femicide in Johannesburg last November. South Africa has one of the highest murder rates for women in the world. Photograph: Anadolu/Getty Images “When some of these things happen in our presence, most of us men tend to look the other way,” said Bafana Khumalo, a co-executive director of Sonke Gender Justice. “You have excuses like ‘No, it’s not my business’. We feel strongly that violence against women is our business. We need, as men, to begin to face each other squarely and hold each other accountable.” The identification of Moselakgomo’s body has triggered an outpouring of grief. Mokoena met her about two years ago, when Moselakgomo joined a running club so she did not have to train alone on Saturdays. “She’s an amazing woman,” said Mokoena. “She always spoke about her daughter. Tsontso always said ‘Bye guys, I have to go, I have to go to my child’. “That’s just an example of how close she was with her baby girl. And she was a really light-spirited, funny and joyful woman, who was kind – very, very kind.” Running clubs around South Africa organised events to remember Moselakgomo and Mokoena said she hoped this would help push the government and police to do more to protect women. She added: “I’m just happy that the world, or at least our country, was standing still for a moment to acknowledge what is happening. Let’s get this out there and figure out exactly what is happening to women.” Explore more on these topics South Africa Women Femicide Africa Violence against women and girls Gender news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed World Europe US news Americas Asia Australia Middle East Africa Inequality Global development
